The poem looks less like a script than a spark, feeding imagined scenes of primitive life that grew out of talk among Florence's humanists. Lucretius's radical view of a world made from random atoms earned Savonarola's ridicule in sermons he preached in Lent 1496.

The two panels are of the type and size once set into the panelling of a room or fixed to the backrests of a pair of cassapanca. Vasari describes small-figure fables that Piero painted to run around a room for the wool merchant Francesco del Pugliese. They were taken away after Francesco and his sons died, Vasari wrote: "nor do I know what has become of them". Whether these panels belonged to that set is still a guess. They are first securely recorded in 1639, in the Rome collection of Marcello Sacchetti, and by 1744 they passed as Mantegna's. Robert Gordon gave them to the Met in 1875. A year earlier, when he lent them to an exhibition there, they were shown as the work of an unknown artist.

details.text: Look at the knot of bodies in the centre foreground. A lion is biting a bear, a second bear is attacking the lion, and a man dressed in a lion's skin is wrestling that second bear. In this forest nothing is only a hunter: the fleeing animals fall prey to one another as well as to the men.

Now look along the bottom edge. In the far left corner a dead animal lies on its back, seen from its feet. Towards the right, just below the satyrs' hooves, lies the bloodied body of a man, seen from his head. Both are sharply foreshortened, a device that recalls Paolo Uccello's celebrated foreshortenings. The man's face lies upside down at the very bottom of the panel, with blood at his throat and a stream of it running from his shoulder.
At the right edge two satyrs with shaggy goat legs push through the trees, the older one horned and bearded. Lucretius denied that satyrs existed. Piero put them in his hunt anyway.

context.text: For decades this Annunciation was taken for a masterpiece by Rogier van der Weyden, and it entered the Met as a late Rogier in 1917. An early challenge, since taken up by others, argued instead for the young Hans Memling, who arrived in Bruges on 30 January 1465. In 1998 the museum's catalogue hedged, calling it Rogier's workshop, possibly Memling. Today the Met credits Memling himself. The design is a free adaptation of the left wing of Rogier's Columba Altarpiece in Munich.

The patron left his mark on the picture. A pair of linked keys (clés unis) is shown on the shield in the stained glass and once more on the carpet, and they belong to the Burgundian Clugny family. The patron was most likely Ferry de Clugny, a leading lawyer, a member of the Duke of Burgundy's Grand Council and a notable patron of art. The painting must be earlier than 1477: in that year Louis XI made Ferry a bishop and the family arms were changed. Ferry founded the Chapelle Dorée at Autun in 1465, and one tempting idea is that the panel was made for it. Whether he first asked Rogier, who died before he could take it on, or went straight to Memling, cannot be settled.

At about 186 by 115 centimetres the panel is unusually big for a Netherlandish painting of its time. Tree-ring study shows Baltic oak, with two boards cut from one tree, and suggests a date of 1456 or later. Before it entered the Met's collection, someone shaved the panel down to only 2 millimetres and fixed a supporting cradle at the back. It was once thought to be the left wing of a huge triptych; it now seems more likely that it always stood alone.

details.text: Look up at the top of the window. The blue shield in the glass carries the two joined gold keys of the Clugny family. The same keys are woven into the carpet at the bottom of the panel, under the hem of Mary's mantle.

Mary's left hand holds a lit wax taper wound into a coil, resting on her open prayer book. The underdrawing shows a different first idea: a tall candlestick stood on the prayer desk, and one page of the book was drawn lifted, as if being turned. Both were left out when the panel was painted.

Gabriel comes dressed in the church vestments of a deacon. Around Mary the room is full of signs about her. The lilies in the gold-coloured jug stand for her purity. The walled garden outside stands for her chastity, and so does the greenish glass carafe on the shelf at top left, since light passes through it unbroken.

context.text: Giovanni Borgherini ordered this picture when Florence had thrown off the Medici and made itself a republic, if the date of about 1528 is right. Proposed dates run from about 1526 to about 1530. Its central gesture carries the republic's politics. Saint John the Baptist, the city's patron saint, hands the orb to the Christ Child. The message is that Christ, and no Medici, is the one ruler of Florence. One reading ties this to a teaching of Savonarola: that the city had moved its allegiance from the Baptist to Christ as its king.

Vasari described the Borgherini picture as having a Madonna, "a little S. John offering to Christ a globe that represents the world, and a very beautiful head of S. Joseph." Copies followed, and some were confused with this one. On the strength of Andrea's studies in the Louvre and the Uffizi, the Met's panel is taken to be the primary version, the one painted for Borgherini. Its later story is less clear. Medici papers record Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici buying a picture from a Vincenzo Borgherini in 1579, while the Met's provenance lists this one with Vincenzio Borgherini, perhaps until 1597.

details.text: Look at the hands around the globe. The Baptist holds it from below, the Child reaches in to take it, and the old man's hand rests on top.
Look at the old man behind the globe, gazing straight out. He is Saint Joseph, and one reading takes his head for Andrea's own face.

context.text: Even a plum tree rotten with age flowers at the very start of spring. That made it a sign of endurance and renewal. Here a single old tree fills four gold sliding doors. Together they made up a whole wall at Myōshinji, the great Zen complex in Kyoto, in a room of its subtemple Tenshōin: probably a reception room where the abbot lived. Each of the room's four sides most likely had its own giant tree. On their backs, facing the next room, was a Chinese subject, the Eight Daoist Immortals. That side is now in the Minneapolis Institute of Art.

The doors are thought to be by Kanō Sansetsu, probably from the end of his career. They date from 1646, or perhaps 1647, the year the building they were made for went up; they were likely finished with it. In 1647 the court also gave Sansetsu the title of Hokkyō. His last years were spent under a cloud all the same. He was imprisoned for a crime he believed he had not committed.

Around 1886, so the story goes, the temple let the doors go to pay for repairs after a fire. They then moved between collectors in Kyoto. Even the black lacquer frames are probably later. One of those owners must have added them when he cut the doors down to suit his smaller house.

details.text: Look at the trunk. It climbs out of the right-hand doors, arches up and left over the middle two, and comes down again in the second door, dark and knotted. Thin twigs spray from it, carrying small pale blossoms across the gold: the old tree still flowering in the cold.
The joins hide a loss you cannot see. At least a foot of painting is gone where the first door meets the second, and again where the third meets the fourth. The tops were trimmed as well.

context.text: In January 1372 Ni Zan was visiting friends at Mount Yu, and he called on a hermit named Bowan. He painted this scroll as a keepsake of the trip and wrote on it a poem in lines of five characters each. His inscription dates it to the day: 19 January 1372, deep in winter. The poem, at upper right, celebrates the hours he spent with friends: 'We watch the clouds and daub with our brushes.'

By then Ni had been on the move for six years. In 1366 he fled his home to get away from marauding soldiers. The Ming dynasty took power in 1368, yet he kept wandering, going back to places he had not seen in twenty or thirty years. He made this picture two years before he died in 1374. It is read as a sign that he had found contentment living as a recluse.

details.text: Count the trees on the near bank. There are five, standing close together, and each has its own pattern of leaves. The ground around them is thick with dabs of moss. This late scroll is more complex and monumental than his earlier work.

Now look at the mountain. Its pale, dry strokes in soft greys were laid down slowly, tone by tone, and the whole picture feels calm. Ni's friend, the scholar Cheng Yuanyou, wrote that Master Ni paints 'as if he were carving a block of ice.'

context.text: Two moments from Genesis share one small panel: on the left the world is being made, and on the right Adam and Eve are already being pushed out of the garden. Giovanni di Paolo is thought to have painted it for a many-panelled altarpiece in the church of San Domenico in Siena, now called the Guelfi Altarpiece. That altarpiece was taken apart and scattered long ago. Several big panels are in the Uffizi in Florence. The Met owns this one and a compact Paradise with saints and angels.

The case for placing the panel in that altarpiece starts from an old description. In the seventeenth century, someone listed three subjects for the altarpiece's predella: the Creation of the World, the Last Judgment and the Flood. On that basis one reconstruction adds two more scenes, Paradise and Hell, to make a predella of five, with this Creation and Expulsion among them. The link is hypothetical, though it may be right. Judged by style, this panel and the Met's Paradise may both date from around 1445.

One later owner was Camille Benoît, a French composer who was also a curator at the Louvre. The Kleinberger gallery's inventory card called the picture Paradise Lost, a nod to Milton's epic. In January 1917 Kleinberger sold it to Philip Lehman, an American banker, for $9,000. Battle was raging across Europe, and a note on the stock card warned that the painting was "to be delivered after the war." It reached the Met in 1975 with the Robert Lehman Collection.

details.text: Look at the great disc God is pointing at. It stands for the Creation of the World of the title. Ring inside ring, it narrows to a round patch of brown mountains and green ground at the very centre, while God's finger points down at its outer rim.

Now look right. The angel expelling Adam and Eve is as naked as they are, marked out only by gold wings and a gold halo. It lays a hand on Adam's shoulder and pushes. Adam turns back toward the angel even as he reaches for Eve, who is already walking away.

context.text: The goldsmith once wore a halo that Petrus Christus never painted. It turned out to be a later addition and was taken off in 1993. Who he is remains unclear. He may be Saint Eligius, patron saint of goldsmiths, who mattered especially in Bruges, where he was linked with several craft guilds, goldsmiths among them. Or he may be a well-known goldsmith of Christus's own time. Saints in early Netherlandish pictures seldom had halos anyway.

On its face the scene is simple: a well-dressed couple picks out a ring while the goldsmith weighs it on a hand balance. Yet the figures are life-size, which is highly unusual. One persuasive explanation is that this is a portrait of a trade, painted to commemorate it, and perhaps to hang in a guild chapel. That would fit the care spent on the goldsmith's face, more individual than his customers', and the fact that his figure carries the most underdrawing. Beyond who painted it and when, very little about the picture is certain.

In 1815 the picture was sold at Frankfurt as a work by Jan van Eyck. It passed through German collections, among them the Oppenheims' in Cologne, reached Philip Lehman in New York in 1920, and came to the Met with the Robert Lehman Collection in 1975. Yet Christus had signed it plainly along the bottom edge: "Master Petrus Christus made me in the year 1449." After the date comes a small mark that appears to be a heart joined to parts of a clock mechanism. He used it on no other painting.

details.text: Look at the round mirror propped on the right end of the counter, against the post of the stall. It turns the room around: in it you see a street of gabled houses under a pale sky, and two men, one holding a falcon. Goldsmiths often kept convex mirrors to watch for thieves. Here it may also carry a moral. A falconer would have been an odd sight in a Bruges street. One reading takes the falcon as a sign of pride and greed, set against the solemn couple inside. Another sees the pair simply as idle young bachelors, the falcon a badge of the leisure class.

The shelves are not just stock. Next to the beads, brooches and rings are things people believed could ward off harm: the red branch of coral, fossil shark's teeth, a cup made from a coconut shell. On the lower shelf at the right stands a crystal vessel with a domed gold lid, perhaps made to hold a relic or the wafers of the Mass.

Follow the balance. Its pans tip toward the couple, which may hint at their future faithfulness, or at the Last Judgment. Now look at the counter on the left, where a red band lies coiled. One reading takes it for a bridal girdle, placed there to stress that this is a marriage, set against the idle pair in the mirror.

context.text: The writing on this boy's tunic might be the only artist's signature on any mummy portrait. Or it might not. It is in Greek, and it names him: "Eutyches, freedman of Kasanios", so he had once been a slave. What comes next is disputed: either "son of Herakleides Evandros" or "Herakleides, son of Evandros". It ends with "I signed". That could be the painter. Or it could be a witness to the boy's freeing, Herakleides or Evandros. Portraits like this were made cheaply, by humble craftsmen.

The method was Greek: encaustic, pigment mixed into beeswax. The use was Egyptian. At death the panel went over the mummy's face, held by the outer wrappings. Sitters in Roman Egypt dressed and wore their hair like Romans, yet took comfort in old Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife. This one has no recorded find-spot, and is dated to about AD 100–150. It was bought in Cairo in 1918 from Nicolas Tano.

details.text: Look at the eyes: dark brown, black pupils, each catching the light in a small bright spot. Under the paint lies a fine underdrawing, apparently done with a pointed brush or pen, hatched where the face falls into shade.

Now look at the ear on the left, his right. The wax texture shows its outline was first painted bigger, then pulled in. The letters below the neckline are in a different, runny paint, which pooled along their edges.

context.text: The inscription on this painting names its owner. It calls the thangka "the precious possession of the holy lama of Changphuk", the learned Kunga Lekpa. It was his meditation painting. He was one of the teachers of Tsong Khapa (1357–1419), the great Tibetan theologian.

The painter is less certain. The painting was made in Central Tibet late in the fourteenth century. It is credited to Mikyo Dorje. Its precision, strong colours and lively line suggest a master's hand. He is known to have been at work in those years.

details.text: Look at the small square at the very centre. Here Yamari appears in his red form, Raktayamari, locked in union with his consort, who is an emanation of himself. Together they trample Yama, the god of death; Yamari is death's enemy and destroyer. Four more forms of Yamari, each a different colour and each also coupled, sit in the panels directly above, below and to either side of that square.
Then find the monk at the far left of the bottom row, in orange robes. He is probably Kunga Lekpa himself, painted into the meditation thangka he owned.

context.text: His name already describes him. Maha means "great" and kala can mean "time": put together, they make him the devourer of all things, without end. The second word has another sense too, black or darkness, and so he is the Great Black One. Few guardians in Tibetan Buddhism are as widely popular.

The Sakya order, which holds him in special reverence, commissioned this thangka in central Tibet around 1500. More than 1.6 metres tall, it is among the earliest and grandest paintings of the subject. It can be related to the fifteenth-century murals that survive in the Kumbum at Gyantse monastery, also in central Tibet. Those murals were probably painted under the direction of Newar artists.

details.text: Look at the bar lying across his forearms, caught in the crooks of his elbows. It is a gandi gong, the sign of his vow to protect the sangha, the community of monks. His hands hold a flaying knife and a skull cup filled with blood, which stand for destroying whatever blocks the way to enlightenment. Under his feet a corpse lies trampled.

Now look to the left edge of the painting, level with the lotus under the corpse. A small pale figure, a white cloth at his hips, lifts a long bone to his mouth. He is Brahmarupa, and the bone is a trumpet made from a thighbone. Even the music in Mahakala's company is played on bone.

context.text: The painter set us high above Golgotha, the hill of the Crucifixion. From up there the land opens out into a wide landscape with room for several moments of the Passion at once, each on its own stretch of hillside. Close to us are Mary Magdalene, the Virgin, John and Saint Veronica with her cloth. On the right ride Longinus and the centurion.

Jacob Cornelisz van Oostsanen, also called Jacob van Amsterdam, came from a family of artists and was its best-known member. The panel is dated c. 1507–10, but its oak planks tell a more complicated story. The youngest growth ring formed in 1486, so the wood could have been ready by 1497, yet the likelier date for the painting is 1511 or later.

It came to the museum from a sale in 's-Hertogenbosch in 1901, bought with help from the Vereniging Rembrandt. Apart from a heavily discoloured varnish and a few retouchings along the plank joins that have changed colour, it survives in good condition.

details.text: Read the hills from the far left. Up in the corner, below a rock, Christ kneels to pray in Gethsemane, an angel with a cross on the rock above him and three figures asleep below. Lower down, he takes leave of his mother. Across on the right, he carries the cross among soldiers.

Now drop to the lower right corner. Saint Veronica kneels there, holding up her cloth with Christ's face printed on it. Gold letters on the border of her robe read ‘SALVE SANCT[A] FACIES NOS[TRI] REDEMTOR’.

context.text: Three kings have come from the left with gifts for the newborn Jesus. Geertgen made them stand for the three generations of human life, and for Europe, Asia and Africa: the whole world as people in the Middle Ages knew it. Mary, the Child and Joseph receive them on the right, in front of a stable built into a ruin. Far behind, in the landscape, three processions are still arriving.

The painter is named after the place he lived: the Haarlem house of the Knights of Saint John, known as the Sint-Jansheren. He painted this panel in Haarlem around 1480–85. It sold at auction in Amsterdam in April 1904 for 3,000 guilders, and by July the Rijksmuseum had paid 3,920 for it.

The arrangement is not wholly Geertgen's own. Hugo van der Goes's Monforte altarpiece, now in Berlin, has been called the strongest single influence on Geertgen's art, and this Adoration follows its overall design. One scholar, pointing to what Geertgen took from it, did not rule out that he had spent time in Ghent. Another called this panel a replica, the repeat through which Geertgen's design has come down to us. The Rijksmuseum catalogues it as Geertgen's own work.

details.text: Look at the oldest king. He kneels bareheaded and holds up a gold cup, and the Child plunges a hand straight into it. Behind him the other two wait their turn: a long-haired, bearded king with a tall gold vessel, and a Black king in a brocade tunic holding a gilded crystal container, a fair-haired boy at his shoulder.

Now look past them at the three processions in the distance. Each seems to be led by one of the kings. At the far left a crowned Black rider on a white horse comes out between the rocks; on the road below the town rides a bearded king in a turban; and over the hill at the right comes an old man in red on a camel. If so, Geertgen shows the kings on their way as well as at the end of their journey.
The large brown stone at the front, beside a dropped velvet hat, is probably not all Geertgen's work. When the panel was given a complete restoration, the rock in the foreground was reconstructed.

context.text: Philip became Duke of Burgundy at four. His mother, Mary, Duchess of Burgundy, died in 1482 and the title passed to her small son, though he only began to rule in his own right in 1494. His father was the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I. In 1496 Philip married Joan the Mad, who stood to inherit Castile and Aragon.

Several related portraits of the young ruler survive, some of them fairly distant copies. Their general resemblance suggests they go back to one official likeness, and the closest to this one is at Windsor Castle. In the entrance room of her palace at Mechelen, Margaret of Austria displayed official portraits of the Burgundian court, among them a small one of Philip in a fur-lined gold brocade gown. It need not have been this panel.

Who painted it is unknown. It was once given to Philip's court painter Jacob van Laethem, and also to the Master of the Magdalen Legend; both attributions have since been rejected. Philip's other court painter, Pieter van Coninxloo, has been suggested for a related version in Brussels. It is dated about 1500, though tree-ring dating of the panel allows use from 1487 and favours 1501 or later.

details.text: Look at the patterned collar round his neck. From it hangs a small golden ram's fleece, the Golden Fleece order's badge. Only the greatest nobles and princes could belong.
Look at the cap. Pinned to its front is a gold medallion with two angels crowning the Virgin Mary. Infrared images show the cap itself was first planned smaller.

context.text: Most of this picture is fog. Tōhaku used nothing but ink on white Japanese paper, and from its shades alone he built a scene of wind and light. Shifts between dark and pale ink show where the light is stronger or weaker, so the pines seem wrapped in mist.

Ink painting usually leans on strong outlines. Tōhaku left them out. He painted pines bent by the wind and dim light leaking through the haze. Coarse strokes sit beside soft shifts of tone. The pine grove was an old Japanese subject; the ink technique came from Chinese painting. The pair of screens, each over three and a half metres wide, is now a National Treasure.

details.text: Look at the darkest pine, left of centre. Its needles are thick, ragged strokes of near-black ink. A step away, other trunks fade to grey ghosts, and that fall from dark to faint is all the mist there is.

context.text: Anthony made his home in the desert, and his legend says the demons never left him alone there. They came as monsters and as naked women. He lived from 251 to about 356 and is generally held to have founded monasticism.

Bosch put his signature at bottom left of the middle panel. He made earth, water, air and fire into a stage for horrible beings: a crush of creatures, some real and some invented, standing for the fears and temptations that dog every human step. The inside shows three episodes of Anthony's legend: tempted and led astray by demons, he finds his way toward salvation in the hermit's life. The life of contemplation is held up as the ideal in an evil world. Bosch painted it around 1500, in the years of his great triptychs.

Most of the time the wings stood closed. Their outer faces show, in monochrome, ordinary people harassing Christ on the road to Calvary, under a moonlit gloom. The triptych's recorded history begins in 1913, at Lisbon's Necessidades Palace. When Lisbon lent it to the Prado in 2016, Madrid lent back Dürer's 1498 self-portrait.

details.text: Look at the kneeling saint at the centre. A woman in a white headdress leans over him with a bowl, but his eyes are on you: he looks straight out of the picture and lifts a hand, a gesture read as a blessing. Further back, in a dark doorway, Christ stands beside a crucifix on an altar and watches.
The left wing tells his ordeal twice. High in the sky, demons haul him through the air. Lower down, two monks and a layman help the half-dead hermit home along a plank walkway, after his flight.
In the right wing Anthony sits apart over an open book, praying. Across from him, at the left of the wing, a pale naked woman waits inside a hollow tree trunk. He keeps his eyes off her.

context.text: The naked young men lounging behind this Holy Family may hold a clue to when it was painted. Michelangelo made the round panel for Agnolo Doni, a Florentine merchant who in 1504 had made a prestigious match with Maddalena Strozzi. Raphael painted the husband and wife too. No other finished panel painting by Michelangelo survives. Its carved frame, probably of his own design, was made by Francesco del Tasso.

When exactly he painted it is not settled. It is dated 1505–1506. Yet those nudes refer to statues such as the Apollo Belvedere and the Laocoön, and the Laocoön was only dug up in January 1506. On that evidence it would belong to the time of the birth of Maria Doni, in September 1507. Other sources put it around 1505, or as early as about 1503–04.

details.text: Follow the child. He is being passed, gently, from Joseph to Mary, who reaches up and back over her shoulder to take him. Together the three bodies build a pyramid that fills almost the whole height and width of the circle.

Now look past them. A short wall runs behind the family, and beyond it naked young men lean on a balustrade. Who they are is hard to pin down, but they seem to stand for pagan humanity, kept apart from the Holy Family by the wall, which stands for original sin. At the right, just past the wall, the infant St John looks up.

context.text: The two dogs at the front look as if they were studied from life. They were not. Jan Gossaert lifted them, along with some details of dress, from the prints of Martin Schongauer and Albrecht Dürer. The upright dog at the lower right is copied straight from a famous Dürer engraving, the conversion of Saint Eustace. Yet its tense, almost trembling watchfulness is Gossaert's addition, not Dürer's. He took borrowed parts and built a composition entirely his own.

No reference to the painting has been found before 1600. By then it was perhaps already at St Adrian's abbey, Geraardsbergen (Grammont), in East Flanders, in a chapel of the Virgin. It was painted between about 1510 and 1515, though one older view dates it around 1506. Gossaert seems to have made it for that church, most likely for Daniel van Boechout's funerary chapel. Another account makes it the altarpiece of the abbey's Lady Chapel, endowed by Joannes de Broeder, abbot from 1506. The two accounts name different men.

details.text: Look at the king advancing from the left in a tall jewelled crown. He is Balthasar, and his name, BALTAZAR, runs around the top of it. Gossaert signed the painting there. He signed it a second time on the silver collar of the attendant behind him, the man in the blue turban.

The old king kneeling at the right is Caspar. His gift is the golden goblet of gold coins that the Virgin holds, with the Child's hand on its rim; its lid lies at her feet, near Caspar's hat and sceptre. Saint Joseph, in red between Balthasar and the Virgin, rests on his staff with his eyes turned up to the angels.

High above, the star that guided the kings shines over the stable, and angels fill the sky. Now look just to the left of the Virgin's head. An ox's horns show beside a dark pillar, and above them a single face peeps out of a narrow doorway. It may be the painter himself.

context.text: A stone ledge runs along the bottom of the picture, a barrier between the Virgin's world and ours. Even so, she looks straight out and holds your gaze, while the curly-haired Child turns his eyes upward. Bellini painted the panel in the late 1480s. Its off-centre design, with the figures set to the right and a view opening at the left, looks ahead to Titian.
Years after this panel, Albrecht Dürer came to Venice and met its painter, by then in his seventies. Dürer's verdict: "still the best in the art of painting."

details.text: Look at the red cloth behind her. It is a cloth of honour, the rich hanging often placed behind the Virgin. Here it has been pulled to one side, and a strip of countryside opens up beside it.

Now read that strip from bottom to top. Low down, the trees in the field are bare. Higher up, the hill below a town turns green, under a pale dawn sky. The shift from sleeping to living nature, like the dawn itself, may stand for death and rebirth.

context.text: The Temeraire had helped defend Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar in 1805, and was known ever after as the Fighting Temeraire. By 1838 she was over forty years old and worth only her timbers. In September that year she was towed from Sheerness up the Thames to Rotherhithe, to be scrapped.

It is unlikely that Turner saw the tow; he recreated it from reports, though one account says he came upon the ship on a Thames excursion. He kept the picture until he died in 1851, calling it 'his Darling'. A would-be buyer reputedly offered £5,000, and then a blank cheque, and was refused.
When it went on show at the Academy in 1839, Turner attached lines adapted from a poem: 'The flag which braved the battle and the breeze, / No longer owns her.'

details.text: Turner bent the facts. The real ship had been stripped of her masts; he gives her three, and repaints her black and yellow hull a ghostly white and gold.
He also moved the tug's black funnel to stand in front of its mast, so the sooty smoke streams back through the old ship's rigging. When an engraver later 'corrected' the tug, Turner was furious.
And the sun sets in the wrong place. A ship coming up the Thames was heading west, so the sunset could not have been behind it.
X-rays reveal a big sail painted where the tug and its smoking funnel now stand: Turner seems to have reused a canvas on which he had begun a sailing boat.

context.text: Two men are hiding in the trees, spying on the woman by the fountain. Her tale is told in Daniel, chapter 13. Susanna is a virtuous wife; two Elders of the Babylonian community try to force themselves on her. The young Daniel brings out the truth, and the guilty men are punished. Here she simply sits in her garden while her maids comb her hair and see to her feet.

Altdorfer let the story run on in the same picture. The giant building is the palace of Susanna's husband, and in it Altdorfer set the trial, with Daniel shown as a blond child in dark blue, standing on a pedestal to question the two elders. Out on the forecourt the elders are stoned.

The panel, signed and dated 1526, came to the Alte Pinakothek from the dukes' art cabinet in Munich. Its palace borrows from Venetian, Milanese and Lombard building, with a lighter touch of Bramante. Altdorfer was a civic figure by then: through 1525 and 1526 he filled important council positions in his city, and in 1528 he was elected mayor.

details.text: Look at the far left, between the trunks. Two small figures in red and blue crouch in the shade, spying on Susanna. To their left, the date 1526 and Altdorfer's monogram are painted on a trunk as if cut into the bark.

Now follow the balustrade to the forecourt beyond it. A tiered fountain stands at its far left. In the middle and to the right, figures lie sprawled on the paving while others stand over them: the stoning of the elders.

context.text: In October 1767 the painter Gabriel-François Doyen told the playwright Charles Collé about an odd request. A gentleman, pointing to his mistress, wanted her painted on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself placed where he could see her legs. Doyen, stunned, sent him on to Fragonard, who took the job; by the time Collé wrote, Fragonard was already at work.

Collé never names the patron. He is usually taken to be a very rich tax farmer for the French clergy, which might explain the wish for a bishop. In the finished picture no bishop pushes the swing: an elderly husband works the ropes, while her young lover lies among the bushes below.

Swings were hugely popular at the time, and not only for fun. Long prescribed for the sick, by the 18th century they were even tried as a cure for melancholy, seasickness and impotence, and were often found in brothels.
By 1865, when the 4th Marquess of Hertford bought it at a Paris sale, it ranked among France's best-known pictures. Six years before, the Louvre had been offered it, and said no.

details.text: Up goes the swing and off flies a slipper, leaving the young man below with a view meant for him alone. He raises his hat toward her, a hint of his delight.
The little statue at the left is Falconet's Menacing Cupid, made for Madame de Pompadour, the mistress of Louis XV.
Swirling diagonals and bright pink set against blue-green come from the style of Fragonard's teacher, François Boucher.

Cleaning in 2021 found little underdrawing: Fragonard seems to have painted straight onto the canvas. It also revealed changes he made as he went, to the woman's knee and petticoat and to the young man's right shoulder.

context.text: According to Vasari, this picture survived a shipwreck. A violent storm drove the ship carrying it onto a rock, and the hull split apart. Every man aboard was lost, and the cargo with them. Only the panel, still safe in its case, was washed up on the shore near Genoa. In recent years, doubts have been raised about whether that really happened.

Raphael and his workshop painted it in 1515–1516. Jacopo Basilio ordered it for a Palermo monastery, Santa Maria dello Spasimo, and the monastery gave it its nickname, Lo Spasimo di Sicilia. In Vasari's day it was held to be a marvel. Later the viceroy of Sicily got it handed over to Philip IV of Spain, who hung it over the main altar of the chapel in Madrid's Alcázar.

details.text: Look at Christ, low in the middle. Crushed by the cross, he has fallen to the ground and turns his head to the women, whom Vasari describes as in 'a storm of weeping'. The crowd is arranged along two diagonals, and both meet at him. That clear but intricate scheme, and the picture's oratorical tone, recall the tapestry designs made for the Vatican.

The Virgin is among these mourners, and the way she is shown took a side in a real argument about what kind of pain Mary felt during the Passion. Following the Church's official view, she suffers and feels for her son, yet she stays conscious. Look along the group: no one has fainted.

Now find the small flat stone in the grass at the very bottom, near the centre, apart from the rock under Christ's hand. It carries the painted words RAPHAEL VRBINAS. One name signs a picture that Raphael made with his workshop.

context.text: In the Spanish town of Monforte de Lemos, this Netherlandish altarpiece once passed for a Rubens. The Jesuits of Monforte credited it to him, and its colour helps explain the mistake: glowing crimson and red set against warm browns and greens. Its real painter was Hugo van der Goes. Berlin bought it from the monastery at Monforte in 1914, and it still carries the town's name.

Parts of it look Italian, too. Cut out on their own, the portrait-like heads at the back could be mistaken for Florentine work. That fed an old idea, first put forward in 1859, that Hugo travelled to Italy before joining the painters' guild in 1467. Against that, it has been argued that an Italian look need not mean he ever went there.
Where it falls in his career is disputed too. Berlin dates it about 1470–1475. One view puts it four or five years before his Portinari triptych; another places it after that altarpiece.

What survives is only the middle of something much bigger. This was the centre of a large triptych, and the old frame still has iron hinges on its sides where the movable wings hung. Both wings are gone. Copies show a Nativity on the left and the Circumcision on the right. Opened out, the whole altarpiece was nearly six metres wide.

details.text: Look at the very top, in the raised middle section. The purple and golden-yellow cloth hanging there belongs to angels who once hovered over the scene. The top of the panel was cut down, so only the lower parts of their robes are left.

The eldest king kneels before the child, hands joined in prayer. On the floor beside his gift on the rock lies his fur hat ringed with a jewelled crown, taken off as a sign of humility. The three kings are clearly of different ages: young, middle-aged and old. That was a motif from the 1300s, read as an allusion to the three ages of man bowing before Christ.

Now find the shepherds, small and far off through the opening at the top, just right of centre, among their sheep. In a fourteenth-century legend they told the kings of the miracle they had seen and pointed the way. And at the lower left, beside Joseph, grow blue irises, a quiet hint of the Passion that is easy to overlook.

context.text: The Annunciation at the centre was probably not made to order at all. It reuses a slightly earlier design from Robert Campin's workshop in Tournai, and seems to have been painted first. Soon afterwards a buyer ordered the two wings, apparently from two different painters, and had himself put in the left one. Later still, in the 1430s and presumably after he married, his wife and the messenger at the gate were painted in. Infrared and X-ray images show the left wing first existed without them.

Even the windows changed. The central panel's windows were first covered in gold leaf, then painted over with blue sky and coats of arms. The shield in the left window was traced in 1898 to a Mechelen family whose name appears as Ymbrechts, Ingelbrechts, Engelbrechts and more; the right-hand shield has been tied, less convincingly, to a family from Düsseldorf. One elaborate theory points to a thrice-married Peter Engelbrechts, with ties to both Cologne and Mechelen. The oak boards tell a similar story: the centre's timber may have been cut as much as twenty-five years before the wings' timber, a hint, though not proof, that the parts were painted at different times.

Who held the brush is unsettled too. Campin, sometimes called the Master of Flémalle, is documented with at least two assistants, among them the young Rogier van der Weyden, who worked in his shop from 1427 to 1432. The triptych is credited to Campin's workshop, about 1427–32; it has also been given to Campin and an assistant, possibly Rogier, about 1425–30. Whoever painted it, its owners would have prayed before it at home, and a conception of Christ in a room much like their own may have fed their hope of children. The wife kneels behind her husband, unable to see into the room, so she can only picture the miracle in her mind.

details.text: Look at the round window above the angel's wings. Sliding down the golden rays is a tiny figure holding a cross: the Christ Child, arriving in person. This homely, rather undignified way of showing the conception drew objections from theologians from the start, and a pope later condemned it.

Now look at the table. A thin thread of smoke rises from the candle, the pages of the open book are lifting, and a scroll has rolled loose beside it. The sudden arrival from the left seems to have just put the flame out. One reading is that the lilies in the jug sit so naturally on the table that, without other Annunciations to go by, nobody would take them for more than a pleasant still life. Putting the Annunciation in a home, rather than a church or its doorway, was a striking novelty at the time.

On the right, Joseph, Mary's betrothed, is boring holes in a board. On his bench sits a small half-made box device, and another stands finished on the ledge outside his window. They are mousetraps, and they are thought to allude to Saint Augustine, who called the cross the Devil's mousetrap with Christ as the bait. The board itself has been read three ways: the lid of a bait box, a strainer for a winepress, or a fire screen. Nobody is sure.

context.text: A line adapted from Leviticus once spelled out the lesson: "Let the balance be just and the weights equal." A seventeenth-century observer saw it inscribed, probably on the picture's old frame. That frame was not kept, and the words are lost. What remains is a couple, a pair of scales and a heap of coins.

Quinten Massys's panel is dated 1514. Yet he dressed the pair in the fashions of Van Eyck's day, some seventy-five years earlier. The picture has been seen as a deliberate reconstruction of that older manner, and it was much imitated.

The man at the scales is a money-changer. His trade was to check the weight of coins and to look at their condition and the quality of their metal. The scales may carry a second meaning too, calling to mind the souls weighed on Judgement Day. The lost inscription makes that reading more tempting, but it remains a reading.

details.text: The round mirror on the counter holds a window with coloured glass, a church tower outside, and a small figure in a red hat by the window. One reading makes this a customer waiting while his money is weighed, but who it is stays an open question. A mirror turned to a window like this already appears in a picture by Petrus Christus.

Her book lies open at a picture of the Virgin and Child, and her hand is on a page. She may simply approve of her husband's honest dealing, or greed may be pulling her away from prayer. Either way, her eyes have left the page for the coins and the scales.

context.text: Why paint a flower this big? O'Keeffe remembered admiring a small flower still life by Fantin-Latour while skyscrapers seemed to go up overnight in New York. Painted that small, she reasoned, her flowers would go unseen, because she was unknown. “So I thought I'll make them look big like the huge buildings going up. People will be startled; they'll have to look at them—and they did.”

The giant flowers startled even the man closest to her. Alfred Stieglitz, her husband and her dealer, was shocked by how bold they were when the first of them went on show in 1924. This one was exhibited in 1927 as The Dark Iris No. III.

From the mid-1920s critics read her flowers as sexual metaphors. She denied it again and again: “you hung all your own associations with flowers on my flower and you write about my flower as if I think and see what you think and see of the flower—and I don't.” The argument has never been settled.
She owned it until 1969. By the time she gave it to the Met, it had already hung there on loan for twenty years. In 1973 one publication even printed it upside down.

details.text: Nothing here is life size. Seen this close, the petals turn into soft shifts from white to grey and ruffled edges you would never stop to notice in a garden.
Look into the heart of the flower: grey-violet folds darken to near black, split down the middle by a thin seam of dark red.

context.text: In 1830 Delacroix's career had stalled: his Death of Sardanapalus had failed badly in 1828, and nobody bought it. Then, during the 'three glorious days' of 27–29 July 1830, he watched Parisians rise up to defend the nation's sovereignty and individual liberty, and saw the tricolour return after fifteen years of censorship.

He set to work in September, swept along by joy, and finished in December, in barely four months. It is at once a history painting and an allegory, with scenes of daily life, portraits, still life and a view of the city. The French state bought it in 1831 for 3,000 francs.
It is his most famous painting, yet untypical: the only time he painted Paris, and the only large canvas he gave to the working people of his own country and time.

details.text: The heart of the picture is a pyramid: the barricade as its base, Liberty as its centre of gravity, and the tricolour as its crown.
The boy with pistols, often nicknamed Gavroche though Hugo's character came much later, runs ahead of Liberty, not beside her.

The restoration of 2023–24 brought a surprise: Liberty's tunic, thought to be wholly yellow, was first painted light grey. Delacroix added bright yellow over it, dense at the bust and thinner further down the legs.
In the bottom left corner lies a worn leather shoe, abandoned in the rubble. Even the curator had not noticed it before the cleaning.

context.text: Who is he? There have been fresh attempts to identify the wanderer, but nothing reliable tells us whom Friedrich might have been portraying.

His clothes show that he is a city dweller who has gone out into nature to enjoy it. He has reached the peak and pauses at the view. Yet we look less at the view than over his shoulder, and seeing itself can be read as the real subject.
Figures seen from behind became Friedrich's way of picturing a personal experience of nature; faceless, they can stand for everyone. The picture is dated about 1817, or by another account about 1818.

details.text: The rock he stands on comes from a drawing Friedrich made on the Kaiserkrone, a peak in Saxon Switzerland he climbed on 3 June 1813.
The cone-shaped mountain on the left comes from an 1808 study of the Rosenberg in Bohemian Switzerland. It answers the distinctive Zirkelstein on the right.
The man stands at the middle of the picture, and the slopes on either side run down towards him.

context.text: Ingres grumbled about the endless requests for 'wretched portraits' that kept him from history painting. At first he refused this one. Then he met the sitter, 23-year-old Inès Moitessier, wife of the wealthy Sigisbert Moitessier, and called her 'beautiful and good'.

That was 1844. The portrait took twelve years. His wife's death in 1849 left him unable to paint for months. In 1851 he gave up and painted a quite different, standing Madame Moitessier in black, now in Washington, then came back to this one.

Along the way the picture went through several major revisions. Her little daughter Catherine was meant to lean against her mother's knees, but could not keep still, and Ingres took her out of the composition. The dress went from dark, to yellow, and finally, in 1855, to the fashionable flowered silk from Lyon she wears now.
Picasso saw the picture in 1921 and never forgot it. Eleven years later he borrowed her hand at the temple for his own Woman with a Book.

details.text: Her pose, head resting on a finger, comes from an ancient wall painting found at Herculaneum. The figure is identified as the goddess of Arcadia, though when found it was known as Flora. Ingres probably saw it in Naples in 1814.

Look in the mirror. Her reflection does not quite match her pose. The little cupid on the sofa's carving has no reflection, though the carving does. Perhaps Ingres was bending space on purpose; perhaps it is because he did not paint her in that room.
The crinoline was brand new, introduced only the year before, and spreads the silk out for display. So was the hairstyle, pulled back to show a provocative glimpse of the ear.
Read the signature. It gives not the sitter's age but the painter's: 76.

context.text: When Balthasar Blumhofer, parish priest at Stuppach and a priest of the Teutonic Order, acquired this Madonna for his church in 1812, it passed for a Rubens. His chance came after the Order was partly dissolved in 1809. The panel had reached the Order at Mergentheim. It is said to have come as a gift from Cardinal Albrecht of Brandenburg in 1532, though no document records when it arrived. There it was repeatedly restored, overpainted in the fashion of the day, and credited to Rubens. Parish records from just after 1812 still say it is supposed to be his. Only in 1908 did art history give it to Matthias Grünewald.

It was made for a feast. Canon Heinrich Reitzmann commissioned an altar of Our Lady of the Snow, the Maria-Schnee altar, as a pious foundation. Its purpose was to bring that feast into the collegiate church at Aschaffenburg, Saints Peter and Alexander. This panel was its centre. One wing showed the snow miracle. According to the legend, a patrician and Pope Liberius in Rome dreamed of a miraculous snowfall at the same time; the year is given as 352 or as 358. That wing survives in Freiburg; the other wing is lost.

Grünewald seems to have turned to it straight after the Isenheim Altar, which kept him busy until at least the end of 1515. Reitzmann's will suggests the Madonna was finished by 1517, the year a payment to a Master Matthew, painter, is recorded. The frame bears Grünewald's monogram and the date 1519, when the whole altar was complete. It is still in the chapel at Aschaffenburg, around a copy of the Madonna.

details.text: Look at the hands. The Child holds a small fruit, and Mary's fingertips reach up toward it from below. One reading makes the naked child a new Adam and Mary a new Eve. In that reading, the fruit of life handed over here heals the Fall that began with an apple.

A rainbow arcs behind Mary, and on a bench at the left stand rows of straw beehives. Both may go back to the visions of Birgitta of Sweden. Behind her, kept firmly apart, lies the world people live in. Their houses crowd the left; a great church, the centre of their faith, rises on the right.

Now look high in the sky at the upper left. A tiny figure appears in a golden glory, among small winged figures. It is not Grünewald's. This God the Father was painted in during the restoration that began in 1926, modelled on the one in the Isenheim Altar. Before that, the spot held a figure of Christ. It was probably no longer original either, but it was authentic, and it was removed.

context.text: Lochner never signed a painting, not even this one. His name would surely have been lost if Albrecht Dürer, passing through Cologne in 1520, had not noted a tip he paid to have a panel by 'Master Stefan' opened for him. Which pictures belong under that name is still, in the end, a hypothesis.

This small oak panel was once the left half of a diptych that folded shut like a book; its painted back gives it away. The lost right half probably showed the man who ordered it, with his patron saint.

It was most likely made for private prayer, in a monastery cell or a home. Today it is Cologne's most famous picture, nicknamed the 'Cologne Mona Lisa' and reproduced countless times. Yet much of its detail is lost in any reproduction.

details.text: Mary wears the crown of the Queen of Heaven, yet she sits on a red cushion on the grass, not on a throne.

Too small to make out here, the brooch on her breast shows a virgin with a unicorn, a creature that legend said only a virgin could catch. The pair mirror Mary and her Child, a hint at the mystical union of Christ and his Church.
Small angels make music and hold out fruit for the Child. Count the instruments: two lutes, a harp and a little organ.
Even her halo carries a meaning: its ornament is a simplified picture of the moon's cycle, joining the study of the heavens to faith.
Up in the corners, two angels pull aside a curtain, opening a shallow space in front of the gold like a little theatre.

context.text: Piero painted this for his family's house in Borgo San Sepolcro, where it hung at first in the main bedroom. It stayed with the family until 1825. Likely painted in the early 1480s, it was among his last works, though another account dates it 1470–75.

While it was still in the family, overcleaning badly damaged parts of the paint, and some came to believe it unfinished. A restoration completed in 2022 recovered much of Piero's intention: the sense of space, the holy light falling on the stable, and the deliberate absence of shadows under the figures.
He set the Nativity on a hilltop near his hometown, as a miraculous vision, following the famous account of the 14th-century mystic Saint Bridget of Sweden.

details.text: Mary kneels before her son. She has spread out her deep blue cloak, her only possession, to keep his bare skin off the ground.
Five wingless angels in loose, draped clothes that recall ancient sculpture sing and play, a heavenly accompaniment to a rustic scene.
Joseph sits on a saddle, posed like a famous ancient statue of a boy pulling a thorn from his foot. One writer calls showing the sole of his foot an unprecedentedly indecorous pose.
One shepherd looks out at us and points up towards a hole in the shed's roof, where the divine light falls. Look also for the magpie on the roof, and finches among the rocks in front.

context.text: Around 1504, a master and his pupil each painted this same wedding. This is the master's version, by Perugino, and it hung in Perugia Cathedral from the time it was made. His pupil Raphael, then twenty-one, painted the subject in 1504 with this altarpiece in mind. The two layouts are alike in many ways, yet this time the younger painter held his own against his elder.

The scene follows the Golden Legend, a thirteenth-century book by Jacques de Voragine. Mary's suitors were asked to bring a stick, and the one whose stick flowered anew would be the fortunate man. It was Joseph's, and the younger suitors were left resentful. Here the high priest, Zaccharia, unites the pair.

In 1798 Napoleon's armies seized the panel from the cathedral, and the French State later sent it to Caen. In 2007 ownership passed from the State to the city. In 2016 it travelled to the Brera in Milan, for an exhibition built around the two Marriages of the Virgin.

details.text: Look just above Joseph's head. A branch with leaves and small flowers rises behind it, the only one in bloom. It is the answer to the riddle of who will marry Mary. The sticks around him are bare.

Now find the youth in red hose between Joseph and the man in green. He is bending a bare stick against his leg, trying to break it. Out on the square behind, a small figure in a red cap stoops over his own stick in the same way.

The couple's hands meet on the same vertical line as the temple's open door. That door is the vanishing point: every line of the square, set out by the geometry of perspective, runs to it. Through it, a bright rectangle of light runs the depth of the octagonal building and opens onto the far landscape. One reading is that this distant view stands for the spiritual horizon the couple are promised to.

context.text: For nearly 250 years the Sistine Madonna was scarcely known outside its church in Piacenza. Pope Julius II had almost certainly commissioned it for the high altar of San Sisto there, probably after Piacenza joined the Papal States in 1512. Only its acquisition for Dresden in 1752–54, after nearly two years of hard bargaining, brought it before the public.

From around 1800 it was copied in paintings and prints, and turned up in magazines, embroidery, advertisements, caricatures and scrapbooks. The two little angels at the bottom were lifted out on their own and began a solo career.

After the Second World War it was taken to Russia, and a legend spread that the Soviet army had rescued it. In 1955 it went to Berlin for an exhibition marking its return, and reached Dresden in 1956.

details.text: Raphael added the two little angels leaning on the ledge at the very end, mainly for the composition's sake.
The open curtain reveals a vision of the world beyond. Mary carries the Child out of the heavens to earth, a kind of image of his birth.
Look at the pale sky on either side, by the curtains: it is made of countless faint angel heads.

Saint Sixtus kneels humbly at the left, Saint Barbara at the right lost in thought; both were venerated at San Sisto's high altar. The serious faces of mother and child seem to know the Passion to come.

context.text: Asked for a title for the catalogue of the 1874 exhibition, Monet balked at calling it a view of Le Havre and told them to put “Impression”. The word was already painters' jargon for capturing an atmosphere rather than describing nature in detail.

The conservative critic Louis Leroy, covering the show for a satirical paper, seized on the title for a ferocious article on 'the impressionists'. 'Wallpaper in its embryonic state,' one of his characters scoffs, 'is more finished than that seascape.' A few days later Jules Castagnary took up the word in praise, and it stuck to Monet and his friends.
The picture became the emblem of the group. It came to the Musée Marmottan in 1940, a gift from Eugène and Victorine Donop de Monchy.

details.text: Monet painted the view from his hotel window in Le Havre, around November 1872, looking over the outer harbour in the early morning.
He painted it in a few hours. The ferrymen's boats in front, the bright orange sun and its reflections were added as he finished.
Behind, cranes, chimneys and masts dissolve in the mist of an autumn dawn.

context.text: The man asked to put a price on this altarpiece decided it was worth twice what Signorelli had been promised. In 1502 a Camaldolese monk named Bartolomeo, a friend of the painter, came to Cortona to assess it. He set its value at 200 gold florins, double the fee the artist and his patrons had agreed. Bartolomeo died that same year; Signorelli outlived him by twenty-one years.

The panel stood on the high altar of Santa Margherita in Cortona, the painter's home town. Its patrons were the lay overseers who looked after the sanctuary, together with the Observant Friars Minor. Signorelli fitted it into a pause in his work on the San Brizio chapel in Orvieto Cathedral, and it was done in 1502, the year he came back to live in Cortona for good. A frame inscription, now lost, recorded the date. Vasari called the Dead Christ in this church "one of the rarest of his works".

Vasari also passes on a darker story. It is said, he writes, that Signorelli's much-loved son was killed in Cortona, and that the grieving father had the body stripped and portrayed it without a tear, so that his own work could give back what fortune had taken. Vasari does not link that story to this panel. Some have since seen Signorelli's first-born son, Antonio, in the dead Christ here; in their version, unlike Vasari's, the young man died of plague in 1502. The likeness remains a reading, not a record.

details.text: Look either side of the cross. Far off on the left, the Crucifixion plays out among mounted soldiers and banners. On the right, Christ rises in a golden glow above slumped guards. The cross divides the panel so that the moment before and the moment after bracket the mourning in front.

Now look past the mourners to the city by the water. The landscape has the careful, closely observed manner of Flemish painting. The mourners themselves are different: their hard, glossy colours call to mind the wooden sculpture groups made for devotion in the same years.

The strip at the bottom, the predella, steps back to earlier in the story. Read left to right: Christ kneeling in the garden, then the Last Supper, then his arrest, and last the flagellation. Between the supper and the arrest sits a small panel of its own, a gold chalice with a white wafer above it.

context.text: Holbein spent years away in England. Back in Basel between trips, in 1528 or 1529, he painted his wife Elsbeth with their two eldest children, Philipp and Katharina.
Elsbeth was left for long stretches to raise their children alone. All three faces look sad, and people have tried to explain why, from a deserted wife's grief to sore, inflamed eyes.

Holbein went back to England without it. Even before his death Elsbeth had let it go: by 1542 the Zurich painter Hans Asper had it. Copies made mostly in the 16th century show how soon it became famous; one, in Lille, is titled Caritas, or Charity.

details.text: Mother and children make a pyramid, like the old pictures of Saint Anne with her daughter Mary and the Christ Child, or of Mary with the infant Jesus and John. Her hand on the boy's shoulder recalls Leonardo, whose work Holbein probably saw in France in 1524.
Yet this pyramid will not settle. The girl gazes off to the right and the boy looks up the same way, toward someone who may once have stood there: perhaps Holbein himself, at his easel.

Holbein painted on paper. At some point the figures were cut out round their outlines, the sheet apparently trimmed hard at two sides, and the whole glued to a dark panel. The date at lower right lost its last digit in the process.

context.text: According to Vasari, nobody was allowed to watch this picture being made for three years. Pontormo, he says, shut himself inside the Capponi Chapel in the church of Santa Felicita, Florence, and kept everyone out, his own patron included, until he was done in 1528. The Capponi family had taken over the chapel in 1525. One account puts Lodovico Capponi's commission to Pontormo in 1526, though the painting itself is dated 1525–1528. It is still on the chapel altar, in a gilded frame carved by Baccio d'Agnolo, and is counted among the landmarks of early Mannerism.

What he made resists a simple label. It is called a Deposition, a Lamentation or an Entombment. Nor is it clear whether the bearers are taking the dead Christ toward the Virgin, who seems to faint, or away from her. There is no cross and no tomb in the picture to settle it.

details.text: Look at the colour. Pinks, pale blues, greens and oranges sit side by side, and there are almost no dark shadows. Vasari said Pontormo, always chasing novelty, painted it "without shadows", in colour so bright and even that lights, half-tones and darks are hard to tell apart.

Look at what is under their feet: only a dark strip of ground, with grey-blue sky behind the crowd. Pontormo gave them an artificial hill like a stage set, a device to explain why the figures climb so high up the panel.
Then look to the far right edge. The bearded man with blond curls and a green turban, staring out of the picture, is thought to be the painter himself.

context.text: The whole upper half of this altarpiece shows hard physical work: the struggle to get a dead body down from a cross. Rosso Fiorentino made it in 1521 for a Volterra confraternity, the Compagnia della Croce di Giorno, whose chapel adjoined San Francesco. The same year he made a panel for the parish church of Villamagna, which suggests he stayed in Volterra at least briefly.

He drew on two older works. The sense of space goes back to a Deposition by Filippino Lippi from 1502. The dead Christ, though, is an open borrowing from Michelangelo's Pietà, which stands in St Peter's.

The panel stayed in the confraternity's chapel until 1788, when it moved into the cathedral, to the chapel of San Carlo. The cathedral still owns it. Vasari called it "a most lovely Deposition from the Cross". Its intensity has also been called disquieting.

details.text: Look at Christ's skin, a sallow yellow-green. For a man taken down from a cross, there is surprisingly no blood running from any of his wounds.
Now find the ladder leaning across at the lower right, behind the man hiding his face. On its foot Rosso signed with his nickname, RVBEVS, and added the date, MDXXI.

context.text: While Moses was up on Mount Sinai collecting the Ten Commandments, his people chose another god. Aaron, the man in the white cloak, melted down their gold earrings to make the idol they now dance around.
The Bible calls it a calf, but this is a bull. Poussin probably meant Apis, the bull-god of Egypt, so the Israelites are slipping back into Egyptian ritual.

Poussin painted it in 1633–34 for Amedeo dal Pozzo's palace in Turin, with a companion piece, The Crossing of the Red Sea. Around 1680 it was apparently sold to a painter buying for Louis XIV. The pair stayed together until 1945; the companion is now in Melbourne.
Centuries later the picture was the target of a deliberate attack, and in 1978 it had to be repaired and retouched.

details.text: Look at the top left. Moses is back, Joshua at his side. Furious at what he sees, he lifts the stone tablets to smash them.

The dancers' muscular bodies and flowing robes come from Poussin's study of ancient sculpture. Turned the other way round, the same group already appears in his earlier picture of a pagan revel. He is said to have posed little clay figures as models.
Exodus says the people were naked. Poussin chose not to show them so: apart from the small children, his crowd is draped.
On the right, tents show that the worshippers have travelled far. A bright light falls from our side; an old man standing before the tents raises a hand to shade his eyes.

context.text: Carpaccio puts the miracle off to one side. Up in a loggia over the Grand Canal, the patriarch of Grado, Francesco Querini, holds a relic of the Holy Cross before a man possessed by a spirit, and the man is cured on the spot. The rest of the canvas goes to Venice itself: its bridge, its boats and its noisy everyday life.

The relic had once belonged to the patriarch of Constantinople. In 1369 it came to the Venetian confraternity of San Giovanni Evangelista, a gift from Filippo de Mezières, Cyprus's grand chancellor. From the mid-1490s Carpaccio, Gentile Bellini and three other painters filled the room that kept it with scenes of its miracles. This one dates from about 1494–96. The wonders were set in real, recognisable places, such as Piazza San Marco or the Rialto, and painted exactly, so that they would be easier to believe.

Within half a century the canvas was cut. In 1544, probably to fit new doors, several paintings, this one among them, lost a strip from the bottom. The brothers took expert advice first. The record says "the very wise Master Titian" came to look, and that he recommended cutting some off the bottom, "saying the cut would not damage the said canvases in any way". A century later the picture was lengthened again by 27 centimetres, and the addition is plain to see.

details.text: Look at the bridge. This is the old wooden Rialto of 1458, and the painting is a rare record of it. Its middle section could be raised to let bigger ships through, and the ropes that lifted it are easy to pick out. In 1502 so many people crowded onto it that it almost collapsed. A new bridge, of stone, went up in 1591 and still stands.

Find the man in black in the loggia, head tipped back. A man in a white surplice and red cap holds a long gold staff with an ornate tip out toward him: this is the healing. To the right, white-hooded brothers kneel or hold tall gold candlesticks. The procession has climbed the steps to the loggia, where the patriarch, the city's spiritual leader, meets them.
Farther along the houses on the left, above a portico roof, a round sign hangs from an iron bracket. It marks an inn called the Sturgeon, and a real inn of that name once did business here.

context.text: Jupiter comes to Leda in the shape of a swan. Around 1532 Correggio painted a cycle of the god's love affairs, in his various disguises, for Federico II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua. They have been counted among the most erotic pictures of the Renaissance, yet not one shows a man of flesh and blood.
Whom they were for is uncertain. Some were reportedly to be sent to the Emperor, and this canvas is said to have gone to Charles V; but the duke may have ordered the set for himself.

Its later life was violent. Swedish troops carried it off from Prague in 1648, and Queen Christina took it to Rome after giving up her throne. In France it came to Louis, son of the Regent, the Duke of Orléans. Offended by Leda, he cut the picture apart in a fit of religious frenzy.
The pieces were put back together and restored. Later it was bought on behalf of Frederick the Great, and by 1770 it hung in his picture gallery at Potsdam.

details.text: Look at Leda's face: it is not Correggio's. Her head was lost and repainted more than once, last in Berlin in 1834–35, when the scene's sensual pleasure was also toned down. At first she faced further to the right.
At the left a winged young Cupid plays a lyre, the instrument of divine music, and a small cupid below him blows a long horn.
Behind Leda, a maid in red lifts a white cloth over a bather climbing out of the water. At the far right, a swan swims up to a standing girl, and another hovers above the trees.

context.text: When Prince William V bought this panel at auction in Leiden in 1766, he paid 7,350 guilders, more than ten times the price of a painting by Van Dyck or Jordaens.

It is the work of two friends from the same town, Rubens and Brueghel, made as a showpiece of both men's skills. Brueghel planned the composition, but Rubens started it, sketching the two figures, the tree, the horse and the snake in thin paint. Brueghel then painted the plants and animals with encyclopaedic precision. Both signed it, though Rubens's share is far greater than the inscriptions suggest.
It is dated about 1615, or by another account about 1617. In 1795 the French confiscated it and carried it to Paris; it came back in 1815, and has hung in the Mauritshuis since 1822.

details.text: The serpent has given Eve the apple; now she passes it to Adam, who will soon eat the forbidden fruit.

Look behind Adam: a little monkey is biting into an apple, and a bird of paradise stands at his feet. In 1621 Brueghel wrote that he was watching and painting the creatures in Albert and Isabella's menagerie.

Brueghel worked over an underdrawing, but moved some things as he painted, like the yapping dogs in the middle of the garden. Rubens's figures show no underdrawing that can be seen: he painted the couple directly on the panel.

context.text: The legend tells of Ursula, a princess and a Christian, from Britain or perhaps Brittany, who went to Rome on pilgrimage with 11,000 virgins. Here her companions prepare to sail home. They carry bows and arrows, emblems of the martyrdom that awaits them: at Cologne, the legend says, the invading Huns killed them all.

Claude painted it in 1641 for Fausto Poli, who ran the household of Pope Urban VIII and looked after the Barberini family's property, shortly before he was made a cardinal. Claude lived most of his life in Rome, and the buildings echo ones he and Poli knew.

The story was popular in the 1500s but rarely painted in the 1600s. In the 20th century the legend itself was questioned, and Ursula's feast day of 21 October was removed from the Roman Catholic calendar.

details.text: The round temple at the left is based on the Tempietto at San Pietro in Montorio, built where Saint Peter was crucified. The museum likens the palace behind it to the home of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, the Pope's nephew.
Ursula, in yellow, holds up a white flag marked with a red cross as her companions file down the steps.
The ships in the centre fly blue flags; the museum identifies the emblem on them as that of the Barberini, Claude's most influential patrons.
As the museum points out, the prows of the moored ships on the right lead across to Ursula, and a pair of noblemen watching from the lower left corner steer our eyes to her too.

context.text: Bartolomeo Panciatichi lived between Florence and France. He was born in France, an illegitimate son of a rich merchant family from Pistoia that had settled in Florence. His business reached as far as Lyon. Duke Cosimo de' Medici trusted him, and sent him as ambassador to the French court.
Back in Florence he married Lucrezia Pucci. In the early 1540s Bronzino painted the couple as a pair, and both portraits are now in the Uffizi.

details.text: Bronzino was prized for his near-obsessive precision, and the beard shows it. Each red strand was painted separately, and the whole is combed into two points, as was the fashion then. Under the black jacket, his sleeves are lacquer-red satin cut with many small slits.
Look at the building at the right. His family's arms hang on it in full view, a public statement of who he is and what rank he holds. To the left, an arch opens on to a view of the city.
The mood is austere, almost frozen. Only the black puppy at the lower right breaks it, looking up as though it has just noticed someone standing in front of the picture.

context.text: Van Dyck's list of pictures for the king asked £200 for "the king at the hunt". The figure was struck out and £100 written beside it, halving the price. That item, paid for in 1638, has been identified with this picture, though the match has sometimes been doubted.

It has been read as showing the king as he would have wished to be remembered: elegant, cultured and needing no trappings to look like a ruler. Charles probably commissioned it, but he did not keep it: it is recorded in none of his palaces, so he may have given it to someone close to the court. It ended up in France, where Louis XVI acquired it in 1775.

details.text: The king has just got down from his horse after a hard ride. The pink garment at the centre of the picture, held by the young man, is the king's own, probably a coat he has just taken off.

Charles was an exceptionally small man, but you would not guess it here. Van Dyck seems to have planned the picture to hang high and be seen from below, which lifts the king above us. The great tree and the horse both seem to bow to him.
At the lower right an inscription names him Charles I, King of Great Britain. It presents a monarch more than a huntsman, an odd fit for a picture billed as "the king at the hunt".

context.text: In 1714 this Susanna was in the collection of the painter Benedetto Luti. He had a copy made and sent it to an adviser of Lothar Franz von Schönborn, asking if the original would make a fit present for the German patron. The answer was yes, and the painting went to Pommersfelden, where it still is.
But it went there credited to Orazio Gentileschi, though it carries his daughter Artemisia's signature. One study ties the gift to Luti's negotiations to be made a knight of the Holy Roman Empire.
This is Artemisia's first painting of the subject, from 1610, and it is still her best-known version of it.

details.text: Susanna is naked and distressed, her raised hands fending the elders off. Her face shows pain, and her refusal to give in to their blackmail.
Above her the two men lean over the wall with their heads together; one raises a finger to his lips.
On the stone at the lower left is a faint painted inscription: the signature that the 1714 gift ignored.

context.text: Rubens painted this view of his own estate for his own delight. A diplomat as well as a painter, ennobled in both Spain and England, he had bought the manor of Het Steen, near Mechelen, in 1635. The picture celebrates what mattered most to him: perhaps his own success, but also the peace and prosperity of his native Flanders.

We can be reasonably sure it was never a commission. Its support seems to have been patched together from small, unevenly shaped panels, probably oak, added and pinned as Rubens went along, a method no collector would accept. It was almost certainly painted as the partner of his Landscape with a Rainbow, today in London's Wallace Collection.
The pair are thought to have hung facing each other in one room of Rubens's house, and an exhibition reunited them in 2021. Constable knew this picture and admired it.

details.text: The sun has only just risen. It glints on the manor's windows and on the gun of the man in front, crouching with his dog to shoot the partridges nearby.
A couple head for market on their sturdy cart, the wife perched high on the load.
Further back, the lord and lady of Het Steen are out walking; a nursemaid holds the baby, while in the moat someone fishes for breakfast.

The picture's size makes us look twice. Up close, we share the crouching hunter's view, though his partridges seem closer to us than to him. From afar, the sunrise on the right marks the east, as on a map.

context.text: To paint this, Rosa Bonheur went to the Paris horse market twice a week for a year and a half. She had police permission to wear men's clothes, to avoid drawing attention.

The picture caused a sensation at the Salon of 1853; one critic felt he ought to leap clear of the horses. In London in 1855 another marvelled that 'so masculine a work is the production of a feminine hand', and it was shown privately at Buckingham Palace at Queen Victoria's request.

After some critics found it unfinished, Bonheur retouched the ground, trees and sky in 1855, which is probably why the date reads '1853.5'. In 1887 Cornelius Vanderbilt bought it at auction and gave it to the Met, where it has been a favourite ever since.

details.text: She painted huge working horses, not riding horses, caught as they wheel round to stride back up the boulevard.
Part of the inspiration was the Parthenon: Bonheur said the friezes came to mind in a crowd of dealers trying out their horses.
The market was held on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, by the Salpêtrière asylum, whose dome rises in the left background.

context.text: After a hunt, Diana has made her nymph Callisto undress to bathe, and finds she is pregnant. On the goddess's orders the others hold Callisto down and pull her clothes away, baring her swollen belly.

Titian made it, with its partner Diana and Actaeon, for Philip II of Spain, the most powerful of his patrons, in 1556–59. The pair seem to have been meant to hang together: the landscape and the stream carry on from one to the other.

In 1623 the two were crated up as diplomatic presents for Prince Charles, the future Charles I, then in Madrid courting the Spanish Infanta. In 1704 Philip V presented them to France's ambassador, and they went on to the Duc d'Orléans. The two British national galleries bought them jointly in 2009 and 2012.

details.text: Diana's right arm shoots out, one finger pointing at Callisto.
Titian kept reworking the group around Callisto as he painted, shifting poses and adding or taking away clothes until it looked right.
Damage has blurred Diana and Callisto themselves more than anyone else; both have lost some of their solidity through paint loss.

context.text: “This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise, with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big,” Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo. The window was in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, where he stayed for a year, 1889–90, hoping for relief from his mental illness.

The picture both records what he saw and breaks away from it. He painted it in mid-June over several sessions by day, not at night. The village was not visible from his window; he based it on other views, and the cypress stands much closer than it really was.

details.text: The sky fills three-quarters of the canvas, rolling like waves. The bright moon is at the right and Venus, the morning star, at centre left.
Look at the church steeple, tall and sharp. It looks like a Dutch spire from his homeland, not a French one.
The flame-shaped cypress shoots up almost to the top edge, tying earth to sky. Some read it as a bridge between life below and death, or heaven, above.

context.text: Wood posed his sister and his dentist as a farmer and his daughter, stiff and old-fashioned, like “tintypes from my old family album.” Behind them is a house in the 1880s style called Carpenter Gothic; he had seen one like it in Eldon, Iowa.
